newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Kabila hitch for Zaire talks, Saturday possible.
newsitem.headline: Kabila hitch for Zaire talks, Saturday possible.

text.p: Zaire's rebel leader Laurent Kabila failed to show for talks at sea with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko on Friday after a day of hitches dogged efforts to bring the civil war rivals together.
Kabila told a news conference in Angola's capital Luanda that he was concerned about security arrangements but had not written off the talks and could attend on Saturday.
"I am worried about security on the ship," he said. "No one has told me about who is there or what their role is."
Diplomatic sources said South Africa's Nelson Mandela, host of the meeting on board the converted Russian-built ice-breaker SAS Outeniqua, was becoming frustrated by the delays.
"We need to stop wasting time," one quoted him as saying.

It was unclear whether the South African naval ship, nicknamed the "The Grey Diplomat", would stay at sea or return to port. It had dropped anchor of Congo's port of Pointe Noire, where Mobutu and Mandela boarded it earlier in the day.
Officials said that Mandela's deputy Thabo Mbeki had returned to the ship to explain Kabila's change of heart and that things would become clearer later.

Aides to the rebel chief said Mbeki, who was meant to escort Kabila to the ship for the first face-to-face talks with Mobutu, was due to return to Luanda to brief Kabila about security measures on the ship.
Kabila said he was also not happy that the composition of the negotiation group had been expanded without his knowledge.
"...And now I've learned that the president of Congo is on the boat. Now this is a surprise. Everyone knows he is a friend of Mobutu," he said.
Asked how his decision not to attend the talks on Friday would be viewed by the international community, Kabila said: "It is my security I am concerned about."

Mobutu, his grip on Zaire crumbling after over three decades in power, is one of Africa's most enduring strongmen -- backed by the United States during the Cold War as a bulwark against Soviet Communism.
Kabila's forces, who took up arms in October, pressed on towards the capital Kinshasa regardless of the diplomatic manoeuvrings and said they were airlifting men and equipment to the war front.

Mandela and Mobutu boarded the Russian-built Outeniqua in Pointe Noire -- Mobutu, who has cancer, with great difficulty. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, Mobutu was driven on board five hours late up a make-shift ramp.
Kabila and Mbeki had been due to join the ship by helicopter in international waters off Soyo by the Angola-Zaire border.
"I am confident the two leaders realise the importance of a peaceful settlement," Mandela told reporters on the ship earlier.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but prostate cancer and the whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on power.
Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in a dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis living there, control about three quarters of Zaire.

Mobutu's camp says the talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow the veteran strongman to stand down with dignity.

Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must stand down and has refused to declare a truce for the talks. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," he said on Wednesday.

A commander at rebel headquarters in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi said an airlift of rebels and equipment to the towns of Kikwit and Kananga began on Thursday and rebel forces were about to enter Kenge, the biggest town before Kinshasa.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who helped Mandela bring the two sides together, has said there are no conditions for the talks.
"In my view this meeting will produce a process that involves a transfer of power and hopefully a transitional inclusive government," he said on Friday.
Confusion over timing has plagued the runup to the meeting, which diplomats see as a last chance to avert a potentially bloody battle for Zaire's capital of five million people.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
